newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Black magic, zombie beliefs fan S-Africa witch-hunt.
newsitem.headline: Black magic, zombie beliefs fan S-Africa witch-hunt.

text.p: A series of suicides in South Africa's Northern Province has led to the arrest of 94 people for persecuting alleged witches they accuse of making people kill themselves, officials said on Thursday.

Provincial state prosecutor Ritshuri Ntsanwisi said that in addition to familiar problems caused by the belief in black magic -- which holds that fatal bolts of lightning can be summoned by witches -- criminals were now taking advantage of the superstition.
In one case a farmer was accused of using zombies to increase his crops, and his corn was burned by rivals.
Ntsanwisi said the suicides of four Giyani villagers early in October had sparked angry protests by fellow residents, which resulted in the torching of seven huts belonging to three "witches".

"Police have arrested 94 people including about 50 youths who are now facing charges of public violence and contravening the witchcraft supression act...in connection with the burning of the seven huts," he told Reuters.
Ntsanwisi said the alleged witches, all men -- one of whom is a traditional healer and the other a farmer -- only avoided being killed by the angry mob by taking refuge at a nearby police station.
They were still holed up in the station, Ntsanwisi added.
"This (latest case) is more than witch-hunt related, it's pure criminality. There are criminals who are starting to take advantage of old beliefs which are still rife here," he said.
"The group also burnt 19 bags of maize they found on (the "witch" farmer's) land. These people said his prosperity depended on the use of dead people to irrigate and plant his fields."

Northern Province -- bordering on Mozambique and Zimbabwe -- is one of two of South Africa's nine provinces most plagued by the ancient superstitions and intermittent witch-hunt killings, officials said.

Recent police statistics show 676 witchcraft-related cases -- which include incidents of arson, attempted murder, fingering people as witches and assault -- were recorded between January and June this year in Northern Province.
Provincial security spokesman Charley Nkadimeng said people paid up to 6,000 rand ($1,310) to have traditional healers "sniff out" the possible culprit.

"We have just gone into our rainy season and are having a lot of thunderstorms. It's an old thing here that when a person gets struck by lightning, you have the whole village accusing someone of having sent that lightning," he said.
